topic: Using Class Templates with Default Arguments
explanation: In C++, class templates allow for generic programming by enabling classes to work with different data types. When a class template has default arguments for its template parameters, you can use those defaults, but you must still explicitly indicate template instantiation with an empty bracket pair (<>). This ensures the compiler treats the name as a template rather than a non-template entity, preventing compilation errors. In real-world scenarios, this technique is useful for creating flexible libraries, such as containers in the Standard Library (e.g., std::vector), where defaults promote code reusability. Best practices include always using the brackets for clarity and to avoid ambiguity, especially in large codebases. Common pitfalls involve forgetting the brackets, which can lead to errors if the template name conflicts with another identifier; to avoid this, consistently apply template syntax and use tools like static analysis.

In real-world usage, such as building generic data structures, this allows developers to write flexible code—e.g., in a library function where users can opt for defaults to simplify calls. Best practices here include explicitly using <> for readability and to prevent errors in complex templates; for instance, omitting it might cause the compiler to misinterpret SimpleContainer as a non-template, leading to build failures. This pattern aligns with idiomatic C++ by promoting maintainability and reducing boilerplate, as seen in standard containers like std::vector, while avoiding pitfalls like type mismatches through clear syntax.
